question: What are the principles of good REST API URI design?
title: REST URI Design Principles
direct_answer: Good REST URIs use nouns not verbs, plural resource names, lowercase with hyphens, and nested hierarchies for relationships. Avoid verbs in URLs — the HTTP method is the verb. Keep URIs predictable and consistent.

interviewer_intent.testing: Understanding of RESTful resource modeling and URI design conventions that make APIs predictable and maintainable
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Using verbs in URIs like /getUser or /createOrder instead of relying on HTTP methods to express actions
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain when to use query parameters versus path parameters and discuss URI length limits in practice

sections.title: Designing Predictable REST URIs
sections.content: REST API URIs represent **resources** (things) not actions. The HTTP method (GET, POST, PUT, DELETE) is the verb, so the URI should only identify what you're working with. A well-designed URI structure makes your API **self-documenting** — developers can guess endpoints without reading documentation. **Nouns** represent entities like users or orders. Use **plural forms** (/users not /user) for consistency. **Hierarchies** show relationships: /users/42/orders means "orders belonging to user 42". **Lowercase with hyphens** improves readability: /customer-orders not /CustomerOrders. The goal is **predictability** — if a developer knows /products, they should guess /products/123 works for a specific product. This consistency reduces cognitive load and makes client code easier to write and maintain.

sections.title: REST Controller with Proper URI Design
Key URI Design Principles
content: **Nouns not verbs**: Use /users not /getUsers — the HTTP method (GET, POST) is the verb expressing the action
**Plural resources**: Use /products not /product for consistency — even single items live at /products/123
**Hierarchical relationships**: Express ownership with nesting like /users/42/orders for orders belonging to user 42
**Lowercase with hyphens**: Use /customer-orders not /customerOrders for better readability and URL encoding compatibility
**Query params for filtering**: Use /products?category=electronics&inStock=true for non-hierarchical filtering and search
**Path params for identity**: Use /orders/456 when the parameter identifies a specific resource instance
**Avoid deep nesting**: Limit to 2-3 levels like /organizations/1/teams/5 — deeper nesting becomes unwieldy and unclear

sections.title: How to Answer in an Interview
sections.content: Good REST URI design follows a few core principles that make APIs predictable and easy to use. First, URIs should use nouns to represent resources, not verbs to represent actions. So you'd have slash users, not slash get-users. The HTTP method itself is the verb — GET means retrieve, POST means create. Second, use plural resource names for consistency. Even a single user lives at slash users slash 42, not slash user slash 42. This keeps the API uniform. Third, use hierarchies to show relationships. If you want orders for a specific user, you'd use slash users slash 42 slash orders. That clearly shows the orders belong to that user. Fourth, stick to lowercase with hyphens for readability, like slash customer-orders. One thing freshers often miss is knowing when to use path parameters versus query parameters. Path parameters identify a specific resource — slash products slash 789 means product with ID 789. Query parameters filter or modify the request — slash products question-mark category equals electronics filters the product list. A common mistake is putting verbs in the URI like slash create-order or slash delete-user. Don't do that. Let the HTTP method express the action. The URI just identifies what resource you're working with.

beats.text: REST URIs identify resources — they're addresses, not commands. The HTTP method supplies the action. Well-designed URIs follow consistent conventions so every endpoint in your API behaves like every other one.

Inconsistent URIs — sometimes plural, sometimes singular, sometimes with verbs — create friction. Developers have to read docs for every endpoint. Consistent URIs mean they guess correctly the first time.

items: Nouns not verbs: /todos not /getTodos — the HTTP GET is already the verb
Plural for collections: /todos not /todo — GET /todos returns many, POST /todos creates one
Path params for resource identity: /todos/42 — 42 identifies a specific resource
Query params for filters, sort, pagination: /todos?done=false&sort=dueDate&page=0&size=20
Nested for ownership: /users/5/todos — todos belonging to user 5; don't go deeper than two levels
Lowercase with hyphens: /todo-items not /TodoItems or /todo_items

beats.text: Todo app: GET /todos (list), POST /todos (create), GET /todos/42 (read one), PUT /todos/42 (replace), PATCH /todos/42 (update), DELETE /todos/42 (remove). Want todos for user 5: GET /users/5/todos. Want incomplete todos sorted by due date: GET /todos?done=false&sort=dueDate. Spring Boot: @GetMapping("/todos/{id}") with @PathVariable Long id, @GetMapping("/todos") with @RequestParam(required=false) Boolean done. candidates miss: /api/v1/getTodo — the 'get' is redundant. GET is already the verb. /getTodo is RPC-style. The URI /todos/42 with GET is REST-style.

items: Verbs in URIs like /getTodo, /createTodo — GET and POST are the verbs; URIs should be nouns
Deeply nested paths like /users/5/todos/42/comments/7 — beyond two levels, use query params instead: /comments?todoId=42

speakable_v2.cap: Nouns not verbs. Plural collections. Path params for identity, query params for filters. Lowercase hyphens. Nest only one level deep. Consistent = guessable.

question: How do you version a REST API and what are the tradeoffs?
title: REST API Versioning Strategies
direct_answer: Common approaches: URI versioning (/api/v1/users), request header versioning (Accept: application/vnd.api.v1+json), and query parameter versioning (/users?version=1). URI versioning is simplest and most visible; header versioning is cleaner but harder to test.

interviewer_intent.testing: Understanding of API evolution strategy and awareness that APIs are long-lived products requiring change management
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Not versioning APIs at all, or thinking you can change response fields without breaking client applications
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Distinguish breaking changes (removing fields, changing types) from non-breaking changes (adding optional fields) and explain deprecation policies

sections.title: API Versioning Strategies and Trade-offs
sections.content: API versioning manages **breaking changes** without disrupting existing clients. When you remove a field, change a data type, or alter behavior, clients built against the old contract break. **Versioning** lets you run multiple API versions simultaneously so mobile apps don't crash when you deploy. There are three main strategies: **URI versioning** puts the version in the path like /api/v1/users. It's explicit and easy to test in browsers. **Header versioning** uses custom headers or content negotiation like Accept: application/vnd.myapi.v2+json. It keeps URIs clean but requires tools to test. **Query parameter versioning** adds ?version=2 to requests. It's simple but pollutes URIs. Most production APIs use URI versioning because it's visible in logs, easy to route, and clients can specify versions clearly. The real skill is deciding **what constitutes a breaking change** — adding optional fields is safe, but removing fields or changing types breaks clients.

sections.title: URI Versioning in Spring Boot REST API
Key Versioning Concepts
content: **URI versioning**: Most common approach using /api/v1/resource — explicit, easy to test, works in browsers and logs
**Header versioning**: Uses Accept: application/vnd.api.v2+json — keeps URIs clean but harder to test and debug
**Query parameter versioning**: Uses /users?version=2 — simple but mixes concerns and pollutes cache keys
**Breaking changes**: Removing fields, renaming fields, changing data types, or altering response structure all require new versions
**Non-breaking changes**: Adding optional fields, new endpoints, or expanding enums don't break existing clients
**Deprecation policy**: Maintain old versions for 6-12 months with clear sunset dates communicated to API consumers
**Semantic versioning**: Use major version for breaking changes (v1 to v2), not for every minor feature addition

sections.title: How to Answer in an Interview
sections.content: API versioning is how you manage breaking changes without disrupting existing clients. When you change your API in a way that breaks compatibility, like removing a field or renaming something, you need a new version so old clients keep working. There are three main approaches. URI versioning puts the version right in the path, like slash api slash v1 slash users. That's the most popular because it's super visible — you see it in logs, you can test it in a browser, and routing is straightforward. Header versioning uses the Accept header, like Accept colon application slash vnd dot myapi dot v2 plus json. It keeps your URIs cleaner but it's harder to test and debug. Query parameter versioning adds question-mark version equals 2 to the URL. It works but feels messy. The key thing to understand is what counts as a breaking change. If you remove a field that clients depend on, that's breaking. If you rename price to total-amount, that's breaking. But if you add a new optional field, that's fine — it won't break existing clients. A common mistake freshers make is not versioning at all, then realizing too late that they can't change anything without breaking mobile apps in production. Always version from day one, and communicate deprecation timelines clearly so clients have time to migrate.

beats.text: API versioning lets you release a new version of your API with breaking changes while keeping the old version running for existing clients. A breaking change is any change that causes existing client code to fail — removing a field, changing a field's type, renaming an endpoint.

Mobile apps can't be force-updated. Third-party clients are outside your control. Without versioning, any breaking change in your API breaks everyone simultaneously. Versioning gives you the freedom to evolve.

items: URI versioning: /api/v1/todos and /api/v2/todos — most common, easy to test in a browser, obvious in logs
Header versioning: Accept: application/vnd.todoapp.v1+json — cleaner URIs but harder to test and document
Query param: /todos?version=1 — simple but mixes versioning with business query params
Breaking changes require a new version: removing fields, changing field types, renaming resources
Non-breaking changes don't need a new version: adding optional fields, adding new endpoints

beats.text: Todo app v1: GET /api/v1/todos returns {id, title, done}. For v2 we change done (boolean) to status (enum: TODO, IN_PROGRESS, DONE) — that's a breaking change. We launch /api/v2/todos with the new shape and keep /api/v1/todos running. Mobile clients on v1 keep working. New clients use v2. In Spring Boot: create separate @RestController classes annotated with @RequestMapping('/api/v1/todos') and @RequestMapping('/api/v2/todos'), or use separate packages v1/ and v2/. After 3-6 months, deprecate v1 — add a Deprecation response header and document the sunset date. non-obvious: adding a required field to a POST body is also a breaking change even though you're not removing anything — old clients that don't send the new field will fail.

items: Making breaking changes without versioning — you'll break existing clients immediately
Forgetting that adding required fields is a breaking change — old clients won't send them

speakable_v2.cap: URI versioning is the standard: /api/v1, /api/v2. Breaking changes = new version. Non-breaking changes = same version. Always plan for deprecation with a transition window.

question: How do you design REST API pagination?
title: REST API Pagination Design
direct_answer: Use offset-based or cursor-based pagination. Offset pagination uses page and size query params. Cursor pagination uses a cursor token for consistent results in large or frequently changing datasets. Return pagination metadata (total, page, size) in the response.

interviewer_intent.testing: Practical API design for handling large datasets and understanding performance implications of different pagination strategies
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Returning all records without pagination, or using OFFSET queries on large tables causing performance degradation
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain when cursor pagination is necessary and how to design pagination metadata for good client UX

sections.title: Pagination Strategies for REST APIs
sections.content: Pagination splits large datasets into manageable chunks so clients don't wait forever or crash from memory overload. Two main strategies exist: **offset-based** and **cursor-based**. Offset pagination uses page and size query parameters like /products?page=2&size=20. It's intuitive — page 1 is items 1-20, page 2 is items 21-40. Under the hood it uses SQL OFFSET and LIMIT. The downside: if data changes between requests (new items inserted), you might see duplicates or miss items. **Cursor-based pagination** uses an opaque token pointing to a position in the dataset. The client sends /products?cursor=abc123&size=20, and the response includes the next cursor. This handles changing data gracefully but you can't jump to arbitrary pages. Both approaches must return **metadata** like totalElements, totalPages, and hasNext so clients can build UI properly.

rows: Uses OFFSET and LIMIT in SQL
Easy: jump to any page directly

sections.title: Choosing the Right Pagination Strategy
sections.content: Use **offset pagination** when users need to jump to specific pages, like an admin dashboard showing 50 pages of users. It's intuitive and lets clients navigate freely. The dataset should be relatively stable — internal tools, reports, search results. Performance is acceptable for tables under a million rows. Use **cursor pagination** for feeds that change frequently: social media posts, notifications, activity logs. When users scroll but never jump to page 47, cursors work better. They handle inserts and deletes gracefully — no duplicates or skipped items. Performance stays consistent even with billions of rows because cursors use indexed WHERE clauses, not expensive OFFSETs. If your API serves a mobile app with infinite scroll, cursor pagination is the right choice.

sections.title: Key Pagination Concepts
content: **Offset pagination**: Uses page and size query params translating to SQL OFFSET and LIMIT — simple but slow on large offsets
**Cursor pagination**: Uses an opaque cursor token pointing to a dataset position — consistent performance and handles changing data
**Metadata response**: Always return totalElements, totalPages, currentPage, hasNext so clients can render UI correctly
**Default page size**: Set reasonable defaults like size equals 20 and enforce maximum limits like max 100 to prevent abuse
**Performance trap**: OFFSET 100000 LIMIT 20 forces the database to scan and skip 100000 rows — cursor avoids this
**Stateless cursors**: Encode offset or timestamp in the cursor token so servers don't store pagination state between requests
**Sort consistency**: Always include a stable sort order (like created-at plus id) to prevent items shifting between pages

sections.title: How to Answer in an Interview
sections.content: Pagination is essential for any API returning large datasets. You've got two main strategies. Offset pagination uses query parameters like page equals 2 and size equals 20. The backend translates that to SQL with OFFSET and LIMIT. It's straightforward and lets users jump to any page, which is great for admin dashboards. But it has downsides. If someone inserts new data while a user is paginating, they might see duplicates or miss items. Also, large offsets like OFFSET 100000 force the database to scan and discard thousands of rows, which kills performance on big tables. That's where cursor pagination comes in. Instead of page numbers, you use an opaque cursor token. The client sends cursor equals abc123 and gets the next chunk plus a new cursor. Under the hood, the cursor encodes a position like a timestamp or ID, so the query becomes WHERE created-at greater-than some-value. This is fast even on huge datasets and handles changing data gracefully. You can't jump to arbitrary pages, but for infinite scroll in mobile apps, that's fine. Always return metadata in your response — total elements, total pages, whether there's a next page. Clients need that to show page numbers or disable the next button. A common mistake is not setting a max page size, letting clients request size equals 10000 and crash your database.

speakable_v2.standard_example: Spring Boot 3.2 REST API for a todo app with GET, POST, PUT, DELETE endpoints
speakable_v2.hook: Never return an unbounded list — pagination is the first thing you add to any list endpoint.

groups.label: Offset pagination
groups.text: Client requests a page number and page size. Server uses SQL OFFSET and LIMIT. GET /todos?page=2&size=20 returns records 41-60. Simple to implement and understand.

groups.label: Cursor pagination
groups.text: Client receives an opaque cursor token with each response. Next request includes the cursor. Server uses WHERE id > cursor_value LIMIT 20. Consistent performance regardless of dataset size.

values: Fast — indexed seek regardless of depth
Items shift if data changes mid-page
Stable — based on sort key snapshot

items: Offset pagination: admin lists, search results, small datasets — page numbers are visible and intuitive
Cursor pagination: feeds, infinite scroll, large datasets over a million records, real-time data that changes frequently

beats.text: Todo app: GET /todos?page=0&size=20&sort=createdAt,desc. Spring Boot: controller accepts Pageable pageable via @PageableDefault, service calls todoRepository.findAll(pageable), returns Page with {content:[...], totalElements:150, totalPages:8, number:0, size:20}. In Spring Data JPA, findAll(Pageable) is built in — zero SQL to write. non-obvious: OFFSET on large tables is slow because the database scans and discards every row before the offset. OFFSET 100000 scans 100000 rows just to throw them away. Cursor-based avoids this entirely with a WHERE id > lastId index scan.

speakable_v2.cap: Offset pagination = page+size, simple, slow at depth. Cursor pagination = opaque token, fast always, good for feeds. Spring Data Pageable handles offset pagination automatically.

question: What is HATEOAS and why don't most APIs implement it?
title: HATEOAS in REST APIs
direct_answer: HATEOAS (Hypermedia as the Engine of Application State) is a REST constraint where responses include links to related actions. A GET /orders/1 response includes links for cancel, update, and return. Most APIs skip it because the added complexity rarely justifies the benefit.

interviewer_intent.testing: Depth of REST maturity model knowledge and ability to critically evaluate theoretical principles against practical constraints
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Thinking REST requires HATEOAS or that skipping HATEOAS means your API isn't RESTful
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Reference Richardson Maturity Model Level 3 and explain why Spring HATEOAS exists but most teams don't use it

sections.title: Understanding HATEOAS and the REST Maturity Model
sections.content: HATEOAS stands for **Hypermedia as the Engine of Application State** — the final constraint in Roy Fielding's REST architecture (Richardson Maturity Model **Level 3**). The idea: API responses include **hypermedia links** to related actions, so clients discover capabilities dynamically instead of hardcoding URIs. A GET /orders/123 response doesn't just return order data — it includes links to cancel, update, or track shipment. The client follows links rather than constructing URIs. This **decouples** clients from URI structure and lets servers evolve endpoints without breaking clients. Sounds great in theory. In practice, most APIs skip HATEOAS because: (1) clients still need to understand link relations semantically, (2) mobile apps cache and optimize for specific endpoints, (3) the added complexity — link generation, relation types, parsing — rarely pays off. Spring provides **Spring HATEOAS** to implement this, but even Spring Boot tutorials often ignore it. HATEOAS is academically pure REST, but **pragmatic REST** stops at Level 2.

sections.title: HATEOAS Response with Spring HATEOAS
Key HATEOAS Concepts
content: **Hypermedia links**: Responses include URIs and relation types (rel) for related actions like self, next, cancel, update
**Dynamic discovery**: Clients follow links rather than hardcode URIs, theoretically decoupling client from server structure
**Richardson Level 3**: HATEOAS is the highest REST maturity level — most production APIs stop at Level 2 (HTTP methods + status codes)
**Spring HATEOAS**: Provides EntityModel and RepresentationModelAssembler to generate links, but adds boilerplate complexity
**Link relations**: Standardized relation types like self, next, prev from IANA registry or custom app-specific relations
**Rarely implemented**: Most APIs skip HATEOAS because mobile/web clients hardcode endpoints for performance and offline caching
**Pragmatic REST**: Industry accepts that useful REST doesn't require full HATEOAS — focus on resources, HTTP methods, status codes

sections.title: How to Answer in an Interview
sections.content: HATEOAS stands for Hypermedia as the Engine of Application State. It's the final constraint in Roy Fielding's REST architecture definition. The idea is that your API responses don't just return data — they include links to related actions. So if you do GET slash orders slash 123, the response includes the order details plus links like cancel, update, or track-shipment. The client discovers what actions are available by following those links instead of hardcoding URIs. In theory, this decouples the client from your API structure. You can change endpoint paths and the client still works because it follows links. That's Richardson Maturity Model Level 3 — the purest form of REST. But here's the reality: almost no production APIs actually implement HATEOAS. Why? Because the complexity doesn't pay off. Mobile apps hardcode endpoints for performance and offline caching. Clients still need to understand what each link relation means semantically. And generating all those links on the server adds overhead. Spring provides Spring HATEOAS to help with this, but even Spring Boot tutorials usually skip it. Most teams stop at Level 2 REST — using proper HTTP methods, status codes, and resource modeling. That's pragmatic REST. If an interviewer asks why you didn't use HATEOAS, you can say it adds complexity that doesn't match real-world client needs. That shows you understand tradeoffs, not just theory.

speakable_v2.standard_example: Spring Boot 3.2 REST API for a todo app with GET, POST, PUT, DELETE endpoints
speakable_v2.hook: HATEOAS is theoretically elegant and practically rare — know what it is, know why it's skipped, and you'll nail this question.

beats.text: HATEOAS stands for Hypermedia as the Engine of Application State. It's the fourth sub-constraint of REST's Uniform Interface. A HATEOAS-compliant API response includes not just data but also links to the actions the client can take next, based on the resource's current state.

The theoretical benefit: clients don't need to hardcode URLs. The API tells them what's possible. If a todo is already done, the response omits the mark-done link. If it's not done, the link appears. Clients follow the API's guidance rather than knowing its URL structure upfront.

items: Each response includes a _links block with URIs for related actions
Links are state-dependent: a cancelled order response includes a view link but not a cancel link
Spring HATEOAS: spring-boot-starter-hateoas provides RepresentationModel and WebMvcLinkBuilder
HAL (Hypertext Application Language): the most common HATEOAS format — _links with self, related, and action URIs

beats.text: Todo HATEOAS response: {id:42, title:Buy milk, done:false, _links:{self:{href:/todos/42}, mark-done:{href:/todos/42, method:PATCH}, delete:{href:/todos/42, method:DELETE}}}. Once done is true, the mark-done link disappears. In Spring Boot with Spring HATEOAS: extend RepresentationModel in your DTO and use WebMvcLinkBuilder to add links. Roy Fielding has said that APIs without HATEOAS aren't really REST. In practice: GitHub, Stripe, Twitter — none of them implement HATEOAS. The complexity of generating state-aware links for every response outweighs the benefit for typical CRUD APIs. production trap: thinking you must implement HATEOAS to build a RESTful API. You don't. Know what it is, acknowledge why it's skipped in practice.

items: Thinking HATEOAS is required for REST — it's part of Fielding's definition but almost no production API implements it
Confusing HATEOAS links with pagination links — pagination next/prev links are a practical navigation feature, not strictly HATEOAS

speakable_v2.cap: HATEOAS = API responses include links to possible next actions. Theoretically self-documenting. Practically skipped by almost every real API because the complexity doesn't pay off.

question: How do you design API error responses for good developer experience?
title: API Error Response Design
direct_answer: Good API errors include: appropriate HTTP status code, machine-readable error code, human-readable message, and field-level details for validation errors. Follow RFC 9457 Problem Details format or a consistent custom structure.

interviewer_intent.testing: API design maturity focusing on developer experience and understanding that APIs are products with consumers
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Returning only HTTP status codes with empty response bodies, or exposing stack traces and internal error details
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention RFC 9457 Problem Details standard and explain why you shouldn't leak internal implementation details in error messages

sections.title: Designing Error Responses for Developer Experience
sections.content: API error responses are a **developer experience (DX)** concern. When your API fails, the client developer needs enough information to fix the problem without a phone call. A well-designed error response has four elements: **(1) HTTP status code** (400, 404, 500) indicating the error category, **(2) machine-readable error code** like INVALID_EMAIL or ORDER_NOT_FOUND so clients can handle specific errors programmatically, **(3) human-readable message** explaining what went wrong, and **(4) field-level details** for validation errors so forms can highlight the specific problematic fields. **RFC 9457 Problem Details** standardizes this with a JSON structure including type, title, status, detail, and instance. The goal: clients can display helpful messages to end users and log enough context for debugging. Avoid leaking **internal details** like stack traces, SQL errors, or file paths — these expose security vulnerabilities and mean nothing to client developers.

sections.title: RFC 9457 Problem Details Error Handler
Key Error Response Principles
content: **HTTP status code**: Use semantically correct codes — 400 for bad input, 404 for not found, 500 for server errors, 401/403 for auth
**Machine-readable code**: Include error codes like INVALID_EMAIL or PAYMENT_FAILED so clients can handle errors programmatically
**Human-readable message**: Provide clear messages like Email format is invalid, not just Validation error — help client developers debug
**Field-level details**: For validation errors, return which fields failed and why so forms can highlight specific inputs
**RFC 9457 Problem Details**: Standard format with type, title, status, detail, instance — use Spring's ProblemDetail class
**No internal leakage**: Never expose stack traces, SQL queries, file paths, or internal class names in production error responses
**Consistent structure**: Use the same error format across all endpoints — clients should parse errors uniformly

sections.title: How to Answer in an Interview
sections.content: Good API error responses are all about developer experience. When something goes wrong, the client developer needs enough information to fix it without guessing or calling your team. A well-designed error has four parts. First, an appropriate HTTP status code. Use 400 for bad requests, 404 for not found, 500 for server errors. The status code is the high-level category. Second, a machine-readable error code like INVALID_EMAIL or ORDER_NOT_FOUND. This lets clients handle specific errors in code — maybe show a custom dialog for PAYMENT_FAILED. Third, a human-readable message explaining what went wrong. Say Email format is invalid, not just Validation error. Fourth, for validation errors, include field-level details. Tell the client which fields failed and why, so they can highlight those specific form inputs. There's a standard for this called RFC 9457 Problem Details. It defines a JSON structure with fields like type, title, status, detail, and instance. Spring Boot has a ProblemDetail class that implements this. A huge mistake freshers make is returning stack traces or SQL errors in production. That leaks internal implementation details and creates security risks. Error messages should help the client developer, not expose your database schema. Always use a consistent error format across your API so clients can parse errors uniformly.

seo.metaTitle: REST API Error Response Design | Java Backend Interview
seo.metaDescription: Design good API error responses with RFC 9457 Problem Details. Spring Boot Java fresher prep.

speakable_v2.standard_example: Spring Boot 3.2 REST API for a todo app with GET, POST, PUT, DELETE endpoints
speakable_v2.hook: A good error response tells the developer what went wrong, why, and where — without leaking anything about your internal implementation.

beats.text: API error response design is about giving developers the information they need to understand and fix the problem. Every error response should have: the right HTTP status code, a machine-readable error type, a human-readable message, and (for validation) field-level details.

A status code alone isn't enough — a 422 just says 'invalid'. An error body with field:title, message:must not be blank tells the developer exactly what to fix. Inconsistent error formats force every client to write custom parsing for each endpoint.

items: Correct HTTP status code: 400/422 for validation, 404 for not found, 409 for conflict, 500 for server error
type: a URI identifying the error class (RFC 9457 convention)
title: short stable summary — 'Validation Failed', 'Resource Not Found'
detail: specific explanation for this instance — 'Todo with id 42 does not exist'
errors array for validation: [{field:title, message:must not be blank, rejectedValue:null}]
traceId: a correlation ID for matching the error to your server logs
Never include: stack traces, SQL error messages, internal class names

beats.text: POST /todos with empty title returns 422 with: {type:/errors/validation-failed, title:Validation Failed, status:422, detail:Request validation failed, errors:[{field:title, message:must not be blank}], traceId:abc-123}. The mobile app reads errors[0].field to highlight the title input. In Spring Boot 3, ProblemDetail implements RFC 9457 — extend ResponseEntityExceptionHandler and override handleMethodArgumentNotValid. For custom exceptions, use @ControllerAdvice with @ExceptionHandler that returns ProblemDetail. non-obvious: include a traceId in every error response. When a client reports error reference abc-123, you search your logs for that ID and immediately find the stack trace. Without it, debugging is a needle-in-haystack exercise.

items: Returning only the status code with no body — a 422 tells the client something failed but not what; always include a descriptive body
Including stack traces in error responses — log them server-side, never send them to clients; they reveal implementation details to attackers

speakable_v2.cap: Good error response = correct status code + type + title + detail + field-level errors + traceId. Never expose stack traces. Spring Boot 3 ProblemDetail follows RFC 9457 out of the box.
